extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literary critics, and students of fiction/narratology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for evaluating and producing fiction with emphasis on narration, authorial voice, narrator reliability, narrative distance, and the rhetorical choices (telling vs showing) writers make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic purity and the rhetoric of fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the relationship between 'artistic purity' and rhetorical elements in fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book frames fiction as involving rhetorical choices rather than being purely 'art for art’s sake'; evaluate how persuasive or communicative techniques interact with perceived artistic integrity. (Page/TOC entry signals a thematic framing rather than a single rule.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling and showing
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between 'telling' (authorial summary/statement) and 'showing' (dramatic presentation in scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess when the work tells vs when it dramatizes; consider effects on reader involvement, plausibility, and moral judgment. The chapter title signals extended discussion of when 'telling' can function like 'showing' and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule I: 'True novels must be realistic'
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation or rule that novels should present a sense of realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how plausibility, consistency, credible detail, and the work’s internal logic contribute to realism; consider how authors meet or subvert the expectation of realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule II: 'All authors should be objective'
rubrics_metrics.description: The normative claim that authors ought to maintain objectivity in narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how apparent authorial objectivity (or lack thereof) shapes reader response; consider techniques that create or undermine objectivity (e.g., overt commentary, satirical tone, intrusive narrator).

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule III: 'True art ignores the audience'
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that genuine art should not pander to audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether choices prioritizing artistic aims over audience gratification strengthen or weaken the work; consider when attending to audience effects is rhetorically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule IV: Emotions, beliefs, and the reader's objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: How authors' manipulation of emotions and beliefs affects the reader's capacity for objective judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate techniques that solicit emotional alignment or manipulate beliefs and how they influence readers’ critical distance. Consider whether elicited emotions compromise or enhance understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of narration
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification and selection of narrative modes and person/point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify narrator type (first-person, third-person limited/omniscient, free indirect discourse, etc.) and assess suitability for the story’s aims; consider implications for knowledge, bias, and intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The author's voice in fiction — uses of reliable commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: How an authorial voice or commentary functions and when a commentator is treated as reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate explicit or implicit authorial judgments and the way 'reliable' commentary shapes interpretation; consider when commentary clarifies vs intrudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling as showing: dramatized narrators, reliable and unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that 'telling' can be dramatized through shaped narrator presentation and that narrators may be reliable or unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the narrator’s presentation dramatizes what would otherwise be told, and analyze markers of reliability/unreliability (inconsistencies, self-contradiction, limited knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliable narrators as dramatized spokesmen for the implied author
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept that reliable narrators can function as dramatized mouthpieces for the implied authorial stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the degree to which a 'reliable' narrator transparently represents an implied author's values or arguments, and whether this dramatization aligns with or obscures the author's rhetorical intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of distance (example: Jane Austen's Emma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Management of narrative distance — how close or far the narrative voice stands from characters and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate techniques (tone, irony, free indirect discourse, focalization) that modulate distance; the TOC indicates case study analysis (Jane Austen) as example of effective distance control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonal narration and the uses of authorial silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an impersonal narrative stance and strategic silence by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess when withholding explicit authorial comment (silence) or adopting impersonal narrative benefits reader interpretation versus when it creates ambiguity or detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price of impersonal narration I: Confusion of distance
rubrics_metrics.description: A potential drawback of impersonal narration: readers may be uncertain about narrative distance and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances where impersonal stance causes reader confusion about whose perspective or judgment is operative; evaluate clarity problems as a risk of impersonal techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price of impersonal narration II: Henry James and the unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Another drawback: impersonal narration can produce or mask unreliability (case: Henry James).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how complex or subtle narrative stances (e.g., in Henry James) may produce unreliable effects and how authors handle or exploit that unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: The morality of impersonal narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical/moral implications of choosing impersonal narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider moral consequences of narrative distance or silence (who is represented, whose interests are neglected), and evaluate the ethical dimension of narrative choices.
